To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the responses of a small population of neurons can be used to measure attention on a trial-by-trial basis; (2) the amount of attention to locations in opposite visual hemifields can be measured independently; and (3) this measure predicts behavioral performance on a trial-by trial basis.

a neuronal population measure of attention predicts behavioral performance on individual trials, and that attentional fluctuations are uncorrelated across locations in opposite hemispheres, suggesting that attention is allocated independently to each stimulus.

the amount of neuronal activity in V4 is a good measure of the amount of attention that an animal is paying to a stimulus at a particular moment in time, that the amount of V4 activity at any moment is not correlated across opposite hemifields, and that the amount of activity at a particular moment is a good predictor of the animal's behavior on the current trial.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how attentional processes are implemented in the brain.
the neural mechanisms of attention.
the neural basis of attention, and we are using the macaque monkey as a model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neuronal measure is a reliable predictor of the ability to perform the task, but it does not predict the behavioral outcome.

attention is a complex process that can vary widely within a single trial, and that the ability to perform difficult tasks depends strongly on the precise amount of attention allocated to each stimulus at each moment in time.
the neuronal measure of attention that we describe here can reliably predict the performance of a monkey in a difficult visual discrimination task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the attentional modulation of sensory responses in V4 is a reliable predictor of behavioral performance on a difficult visual task.
the attentional modulation measured in single neurons can be used to predict behavior on an individual-trial basis and that attentional allocation to different stimuli can be independent.
the attentional modulation of neuronal activity is sufficient to account for the behavioral improvement that is observed in a difficult psychophysical detection task.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the responses of a small population of neurons can be used to measure attentional fluctuations in a way that can be related to behavior.
neuronal population responses can be used to identify and characterize the moment-to-moment fluctuations in the allocation of attention that are likely present in all laboratory studies.
neuronal measures of attention can be used to identify attentional states on a moment-by-moment basis and can predict changes in behavior on individual trials.
